n: The most-quoted Old Testament verse in the New Testament. ‘The LORD’ (Jehovah) speaks to David’s ‘Lord’ (adon, master). Jesus used it to show the Messiah is more than David’s son — he is David’s Lord, exalted to God’s right hand.

f.w: The LORD said unto my Lord

n: From Zion, God will extend the king’s scepter — his royal power. He will rule even in the middle of his enemies.
A difficult verse. On the day the king’s power is displayed, his people will volunteer freely, dressed in holy splendor. His youthful strength is renewed like dew born from the dawn.

f.g: Freewill offerings — they give themselves gladly.
Fresh vigor, like morning dew; possibly ‘your young warriors.’

n: God swears an oath: this king is a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek — the king-priest of Salem who blessed Abraham. Hebrews applies this to Christ. Latter-day Saints also hold the Melchizedek Priesthood, named for this ancient high priest.
The Lord at the king’s right side will crush rulers on the day of his wrath. The roles of God and his anointed blend together.

f.w: in the day of his wrath

n: He will judge the nations and defeat their leaders across the earth — vivid ancient battle imagery for God’s final victory over evil.

f.w: He shall judge among the heathen

f.g: Rulers, or ‘the head’ — a chief enemy.

n: Refreshed by drinking from a stream along the way, the victorious king lifts his head in triumph. Some see a hint of the Messiah’s suffering and exaltation.

f.g: Rise in renewed strength and victory.
